subsubtopic: PROPOSED STUDY OF PROBLEMS OF INDUSTRY CONCERNING DEVELOPMENT AND IMPLEMENTATION OF ANTI-POLLUTION DEVICES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of commissioning a special study, in co-operation with the provinces, to investigate the problems of Canadian industry concerning the development and inplementa-tion of anti-pollution devices.
He said: Mr. Speaker the voice of the environmentalist has scarcely been heard in this House and in the land in the last days of this year. Concern is still felt by many, but the voice of the environmentalist has currently been lost in the tumult of louder voices raised in alarm throughout
Anti-pollution Devices Study the industrial world that we may not have adequate energy resources. So anxious have we been to maintain the materialistic idea of ever-increasing production that we tend to forget the price paid in ever-increasing pollution.
I suggest it is fitting at this season of Christmas, on the threshold of the new year, that we pause to think of the future of Canada, not only as a nation that could with its still unexploited and unexplored energy riches be among the first nations of the world industrially but as a nation that could be among the first nations of the world in developing the anti-pollution and environmental controls which must be developed if the world is not to choke in its wastes. Some beginnings have been made by the federal government such as the Clean Air Act, the Canada Water Act, amendments to the Canada Shipping Act regarding marine pollution, and others. But the board to be established under the energy supplies emergency bill could destroy the purpose toward which we have been working. This board will have the right to make regulations that will take away the effect of all our environmental laws already in existence. This is another reason for the caution that has been expressed on this side of the House about the powers being given under the proposed bill.
The effects of industry on our environment, even in this new land of ours, are noticeable, especially among our mining areas, forestry areas, hydro electric developments, and areas where gas and oil resources are found. But in the tumult over the energy crisis is responsibility to be disregarded? What about the active co-operation with the provinces and the United States that was the cry in the land a few months ago?
Pollution knows no boundaries. Concern must be expressed, felt and acted upon at all levels. Through the measure I propose, once again we would activate that concern and we would co-operate with such bodies as the ministry of the environment in Ontario and make certain, through the combined power of the provinces and the federal government, that legislation that all concerned people agree should be passed for our future will be passed through such co-operation. While so many nations have a past that corrupts their future, the future of Canada is still to be achieved in our own terms. No matter the mistakes of the past, the future is as broad and uncorrupted as is most of the land. We in this land are masters of our own destiny. What is to be is what we choose to make it.
So I hope for the support of all parties in the House for my modest proposal that in the opinion of this House the government should consider the advisability of commissioning a special study in co-operation with the provinces to investigate the problems of Canadian industry concerning the development and implementation of anti-pollution devices. Canada, unique among most of the modern nations, has adequate energy resources and a unique responsibility to use them well so that generations ahead can say "well done". Otherwise, we will be cursed for corrupting our heritage.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED STUDY OF PROBLEMS OF INDUSTRY CONCERNING DEVELOPMENT AND IMPLEMENTATION OF ANTI-POLLUTION DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member on the motion he has brought forward. It is very timely and I am sure

December 20, 1973
Anti-pollution Devices Study concerns Canadians in all walks of life. As the hon. member has indicated, what concerns us particularly is the need for pollution controls that will take into consideration the present emergency with regard to all forms of energy and the difficulties that have been created by the inability of the government or industry in general to provide proper pollution controls.
It is interesting to note that a new automobile built according to 1975 pollution control standards has a considerably reduced mileage per gallon of gas and at the same time the pollution control device installed on the car has a short lifespan. I have heard-and I think that the minister responsible for the National Research Council should have taken a look at the effects of pollution control-that some of the imported cars will have a catalystic pollution control unit using a totally different type of catalyst. It has been indicated by the Nader organization in the United States that the emissions from those catalysts might be much more toxic and noxious than the gases that are currently being emitted by our automobiles.
It seems to me that the government should have provided pollution controls long ago to reduce toxic automobile emissions and at the same time maintained a degree of efficiency in the conservation of one of our major fuel sources. This could be easily accomplished, of course, by reducing the size of automobile engines. The other day I was in one of the oil capitals of Canada where I was offered a ride in a 1974 General Motors half ton truck. I was interested to find that the truck had a 455 horsepower engine and that the mileage the driver got from that brand new truck, which had about 1,500 miles on it, was only eight miles to the gallon. He is getting eight miles to the gallon and the control devices on the truck reduce pollution by 50 per cent. It would seem to be very simple arithmetic that if we went back to the 65 horsepower motors we had in the late 1950's the driver could probably get 30 miles to the gallon from that vehicle.
It seems to me we have been ridiculous in the demands we have made which have almost eliminated any efficiency that could be obtained through normal type of engine development for vehicular traffic. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, the efficiency of pollution devices is of very short duration. What really concerns me, however, is that recently the Minister of Transport and Communications for the province of Ontario publicly recommended that people remove pollution control devices from their automobiles in order to conserve gasoline. I hope that will not be the solution. I agree with the previous speaker that it is absolutely essential that we continue to control pollution in Canada.
One of the greatest pollutants, of course, is the automobile internal combustion engine. I believe that if we really put our minds to it and utilize the resources of the National Research Council to develop proper controls we would be able to eleminate efficiently more of the pollution that takes place.
Until recently on the North American continent it was difficult to believe that pollutants, which are by-products of basic production in the woodworking industry, mining and smelting or a by-product of urbanization, with gar-

bage being a great problem, are in themselves almost as valuable as the basic commodity which in the first place emitted the pollutant. For years in the Sudbury district the emphasis was on employing people in mining nickel and smelting the raw material in that area at as cheap a rate as possible. For miles around, and particularly throughout Blizzard Valley, crops were destroyed annually. As the public began to mount opposition and as the government became more and more involved in lawsuits, steps were taken to make it mandatory that Inco eliminate as much sulphur pollution as possible. That sulphur in itself has now become a valuable by-product. Thousands and thousands of tons of sulphuric acid are now exported from the Sudbury area.
The same is true of almost any pollutant. Rather than disseminating it through the air, in water or into the land it can be developed into a valuable product. One of our greatest future assets in heating cities like Toronto and Montreal will be the separation of bio-degradable waste from cans, bottles and other reclaimable items in garbage. Already this is being used to create energy in certain areas, and the sale of that energy from waste will probably pay for the handling process.
As Canadians and people throughout, the world become more and more concerned about the pollution problem I believe that economic uses will be found for pollutants and that they will become a valuable new resource for development by secondary industry. Here I think of the steps already taken in countries like Japan. I can remember the Japanese efforts in their early days of waste reclamation. Our country used to be covered with tin cans, particularly oil cans. As a child I remember getting a Christmas toy and on the inside you could still see the painted name of Imperial Oil of Canada. The can had been turned inside out, manufactured into a toy and returned as a valuable commodity.
I congratulate the hon. member for York East on bringing this matter forward today. I sincerely hope that departmental officials, both in the field of science and the field of trade and commerce, will give serious consideration to providing the technical know-how to all types of industry in Canada and will undertake further research into pollution emission from automobiles so that what is now a pollutant, what is now dangerous to health, what is now dangerous to our environment can be made in itself productive and become a useful, worth-while product. If we fail to do this, then within a very short period of time not only will we have a crisis in energy but also a crisis in iron, in nickel, in food materials, in fertilizer, and in fact in all the basic resources of the country and of the world.
I believe we have the know-how to eliminate many pollutants. We have the know-how to recycle and make valuable what today are dangerous and obnoxious pollutants affecting the very life style of our people. But if we are not willing to undertake the necessary action until we reach a crisis stage we will fail many generations yet to come.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say a few words about the motion on pollution introduced by the member for York East (Mr. Arrol).

We all know what can contribute to pollution. We also know what are the means to be taken to prevent or eradicate it. Several factors contribute to pollution. Buses, for example, could surely be electrified. Buses are operating with fuel whose chemical disintegration gives rise to pollution. All buses could be electrified and would thus contribute to the removal of pollution.
Mr. Speaker, one municipality is now spending $500,000 on a lake shore in order to eliminate pollution. Meanwhile, it picks up waste, snow mixed with a lot of salt and every kind of dirt that can be found in a municipality and throws that in the very stream where people get their drinking water. It has already picked a quarrel with some company, pretexting that they were throwing wastes into a lake and polluting the water. The same municipality, having made representations before that company to eliminate pollution, has imposed penalties to it through the provincial government while the municipality itself causes pollution because it throws all its wastes into the water. And nobody worries about that.
In my view, laws and regulations should also apply to municipalities that contribute to pollution while calling for its elimination. A great many municipalities in Canada dump snow mixed with salt into streams. This contributes greatly to water pollution and is harmful to fish. All communities located on the shores of lakes surrounded by cottages and buildings where people live should have their own sewage systems. In most cases, raw sewage is dumped into waterways. To treat it would involve spending hundreds of millions of dollars everywhere in Canada. Mr. Speaker, we are always up against the same difficulty: the necessary funds are lacking.
At the present time, the federal government shares part of these costs with provincial and local governments. However, Mr. Speaker, this can hardly improve the situation. Indeed, the debts and taxes of rate payers are increasing and they are too high already. So that is not the solution to the problem.
To solve the problem, Mr. Speaker, as we often say in our speeches, since this is public property and aimed at helping people and getting pollution out of our waters or off the shores of our streams, funds would absolutely have to be made available at very low interest rates. Governments would have to open their eyes and ears and make funds available at very low interest rates. At present governments themselves are borrowing at 9 to 10 per cent, and municipalities at 10 to 12 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, that does not make sense. That is how municipalities become endebted, municipalities or public bodies are prevented from intervening to get rid of pollution. Mr. Speaker, we have that all across Canada. Everywhere there are projects to be carried out but we cannot do that because we do not have the necessary funds or because the debts of both municipal, provincial and federal governments are so high that nothing seems to be worth undertaking anymore.
I would have another suggestion to make to get rid of pollution. In cities we could run cars on the same sources of electric power as buses which would contribute to eliminating a lot of pollution. There is no shortage of
Anti-pollution Devices Study electrical energy in any of the Canadian provinces, and especially not in Quebec. There is an abundance of it and, as the means to produce it are many, it could be used for automobile propulsion.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if governments were willing to go further, they could make available to scientists the necessary capital, at a low rate of interest, at administrative cost, and thus enable them to do research with a view to equipping cars with electrical power and making them operate on dry batteries. There certainly must exist, even now, inventions to make automobiles run on electrical power; this would eliminate pollution to a large extent. Mr. Speaker, the present oil shortage could be corrected this way.
There are a number of other means to alleviate the oil shortage. We could suggest allotting the required capital to developing new types of energy. In a few years, nearly all pollution would be eliminated in Canada. Then, in all our cities, we would live as before the advent of modern times and new technology.
We are not against technology, quite the opposite, we are for its progress, we want to make use of it. But, Mr. Speaker, we can use it without poisoning ourselves and others and without poisoning the atmosphere for the future generations and the fauna of our beautiful country.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I thank and congratulate the hon. member who moved this motion. 1 am sure that other members have a lot to say and to suggest on this subject. It is all very well to make suggestions, but it is even better to put them in practice.
I urge the government, through the work of the committees for instance, to find a way to stop pollution and especially to finance these projects aimed at the welfare of the population.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission I would like to take part in this debate and congratulate the hon. member for having introduced this motion. It gives us an opportunity to examine those things we have been speaking about for so long and to bring them forward in this forum where hopefully some of the devices we know about may gather the attention they deserve.
With your permission and with the permission of the mover of the motion I should like to enlarge the somewhat narrow interpretation of one word in his motion, namely, "devices". I feel that I have his permission to do so, and with your permission I would expand it to include not just an attachment to the various means of locomotion we now have or an attachment to chimneys that emit smoke but actual vehicles.

At the same time, I should like to thank the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Latulippe) who did such a good job in preparing the way for my comments. As a matter of fact, I was just thinking of using a car developed in British Columbia by engineers of the University of British Columbia and which was given a name which is very famous in those circles, that of Dr. Walter Gage. The car is now called the "Wally Wagon".
So, Mr. Speaker-
8948

December 20, 1973
Anti-pollution Devices Study
[ English]
The Wally Wagon was developed by the engineering faculty of the University of British Columbia precisely with this view in mind. A group of mechanical engineers, chemists, physicists and metallurgists, because of the technologies involved, designed an engine. They designed the sort of panels that would be required to develop that engine in the most economical way with the maximum utilization of every conceivable idea of anti-pollution devices. The Wally Wagon was granted a prize last year at a convention in Detroit at which there were a number of other devices and vehicles. It was given the prize for the best design and the most economical car developed from the point of view of anti-pollution devices.
The hon. member for Compton (Mr. Latulippe) suggested that automobiles in urban areas be run on electricity. He lives in one of the fortunate provinces, as do I, where all electricity is developed by hydro power. As hon. members know, there are parts of the country which have to rely on oil and coal for the development of electricity. Therefore we have to ask ourselves whether we are really being anti-pollutionists by urging the creation of power by coal and oil to run cars which do not run on oil or oil products.
The Wally Wagon is powered by an engine which runs on liquid gas. The carburetor or mechanics that go into the conversion of this liquid gas to provide the mode of power have been taken into account with the result that emission from the Wally Wagon is reduced to the absolute minimum. It is indeed a low pollution vehicle.
There is another form of pollution. Our large cities are being polluted by the physical presence of vehicles. It is very difficult to find a parking space. We should get rid of this type of pollution as well.
The Wally Wagon is a very small car. Its measurements are approximately eight feet long and five and a half feet high. Two or three of these could be parked in the area required to park a large car.
This is another form of pollution that would not be beyond the definition of anti-pollution devices contained in the proposed resolution of my colleague. In this particular stream of thought I suggest we might consider such a small vehicle or a better developed one like it, with its production base not only in Canada but, with luck, in my province, as a means of dealing with our urban transportation problems. We could park our vehicles outside our large urban areas. We could get in such a car, put in a 25 or 50 cent piece, drive to town and park it somewhere. There would be a lot of parking places. It would not be a personal car but a community-owned vehicle. If there were another 10 minutes on it, someone could take it for that 10 minutes but would have to produce another quarter to get them to where their personal vehicle was parked. I suggest that it be coin operated.
The hon. member for Compton talked about capital accumulation. I am not thinking in terms of government assistance. I believe there are pools of capital in this country that could be used for the development of a device of this sort. We should use the resources of our country. We have them all ranging from steel to our petrochemical

industries. Many of the panels and other pieces of modern vehicles are indeed manufactured from derivatives of our petroleum resources.
I suggest this would be an excellent way of decentralizing our industry. I am sure all members who have flown from the west to the central provinces have noticed great areas covered with a haze of pollution. It is time we cut down on this pollution which is becoming the bane of the large cities. It is derived to a considerable extent from industry of a variety of sorts. Industry must be decentralized. This would decentralize pollution and making it a little less onerous for areas that now have heavy pollution.
I comment the hon. member for his initiative in bringing forward this resolution. I urge the government to consider seriously his recommendation that a study be undertaken in this area leading to the development of practical instruments which will reduce more and more the pollution that is besetting us.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: PROPOSED STUDY OF PROBLEMS OF INDUSTRY CONCERNING DEVELOPMENT AND IMPLEMENTATION OF ANTI-POLLUTION DEVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to enter this debate. However, I was tempted to do so by the speech of my colleague a few moments ago. He spoke of the importance of auto emission with regard to the matter before the House and how it must be studied. It must be studied from two points of view. It must ensure that devices used on motor vehicles are sufficient, and I emphasize that word, for the purpose of protecting our atmosphere and our environment from pollution. We have to examine the devices to ensure that we are not overdoing in a quantitive sense the capability of the auto emission control devices, particularly at a time when we may be faced with a shortage of petroleum products.
I do not suggest that we panic, run the other way and advocate the removal of all these devices from cars. I think they are very valuable. However, the aspect of research suggested in the motion might be an opportunity to ascertain the true worth of these devices in Canadian terms, whether our requirement is such that control ought to be as stringent as in other jurisdictions and whether the potential danger is as great. We have a tendency to follow, but I believe there is an opportunity for this country to lead in a field that is very important to us.
I am sure that when my hon. friend talked about research into the development and implementation of anti-pollution devices he did not intend us to think only in terms of the mechanical aspect of those devices. It is fair to say that the speed with which the installation of antipollution devices is demanded by the community will have a great bearing on the cost to the industries and businesses concerned. I think it is unfair to businesses generally to demand the expensive installation of anti-pollution devices overnight without at the same time developing some form of compensation to them. By this I do not mean outright payments, although it might well come to that; I do not necessarily mean a grant, although it may turn out to be that, or a combination of the two. I am thinking in terms of a tax incentive or some such mechanism. If the public wants pollution control, if people want to stop the pollution of rivers and streams, they must not burden too greatly the productive capacity of the industries con-
December 20, 1973

cerned, some of which are having trouble continuing their operations. Some assistance should be given in a meaningful way to business and industry, to businesses and industries which are being forced by circumstances or may be forced by circumstances to instal expensive pollution control devices.
I do not believe we have considered the question of public transportation as an integral part of the whole subject of pollution control and as one which therefore requires urgent attention. Only yesterday in Ottawa the Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton announced a planning study, one of a series, indicating it will probably be ten years before the national capital gets a rapid transit system.

As a member representing the national capital area I am absolutely appalled by the length of this period. It has even been suggested the development of the system might take longer than ten years, that it might take 19 years. If we are to be strangled in the downtown area because of congestion aggravated by traffic fumes, as I think we shall, it is criminal that the planning study should consider a period of ten years as a minimum. It is criminal that no leadership is being shown by the federal government in the national capital so as to ensure that the capital offers an example of what a modern transport facility could provide. Surely, as the motion suggests, we are bound to consider the needs of a changing community. Surely to God we ought not to be told in this area that we must wait for ten years before the pollution problem is dealt with and that in the meantime we are to be stuck with diesel fuel burning buses giving limited services on narrow streets. If the regional municipality accepts the findings of that report they are not worth the powder to blow them to blazes. For its part, the government of Canada should recognize it has responsibility to take the lead, by using the tri-level committee it has established, to ensure that the time period I have mentioned is cut down. It is tragic that after having the apple of a reasonable transportation system held out to us we should now be called on to wait for so long a period.
There is still time to avoid following courses of action which have all but destroyed older cities in other countries. In terms of transportation in this and similar cities we are still thinking of a system which is akin to the horse and buggy. Perhaps as a result of the wording of the motion before us other cities will not be plagued by the lack of modern services. I do not know of anything in a modern urban city that is more important than public transportation if a city is to be a good place in which to live, a place to enjoy and a place in which to raise a family. I do not know why the downtown areas have to be the scene of traffic congestion. There is still time in this country to correct the errors of the past, and possibly the device suggested by my hon. friend in his motion is one means of making progress. Surely, in the national capital, some leadership ought to be shown.
I think it is axiomatic that we must look to other forms of energy which will not pollute the atmosphere. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has talked about solar
Anti-pollution Devices Study energy. I wonder how advanced and concentrated is the effort being made in this area. I suspect that on examination one would find that these efforts are scattered and sporadic. Ontario possesses what is perhaps one of the world's finest hydroelectric systems. A tremendous electrical industry is being built up in Quebec. Perhaps in time we shall not be dependent on non-renewable resources. Consideration has been given to using manure as an alternative source of energy.
Hon. members who come from metropolitan areas, or close to them, know the idea has developed that garbage from any one of our cities can be shipped out and dumped somewhere else, or used as fill. There is right now under consideration in the Department of the Environment a technical process, imported from Europe, the like of which is not known on the North American continent. An announcement is supposed to be coming at some time with respect to use of process for the national capital area on a trial basis. The federal government has indicated its intention to contribute to it. I think it could mark a new departure in garbage disposal and the production of industrial energy into the bargain. I wish the federal government would get on with the project. They have taken the position that they wish to lead, and I ask them to lead, not in the partisan sense but in the sense of the importance of this process to the community.
I do not think there is any matter more important to us when we remember that our environment, whether the air, our water or our land, is a very fragile thing and that we have abused it. I suppose this always happens in a nation that thinks in terms of building rather than conserving. Perhaps since the general environment is irreplaceable, and in view of the factors that I have mentioned, we should now think of conserving. I think my colleague has done a great service to us who sit in this House and to the country in bringing forward this proposal, which I am delighted to support.

Take, for example, oil spills. The Coastguard hastened to tell us we had much better clean-up methods than they had thought of in the United States. I refer to those used off the coast of Nova Scotia near Halifax, and I think the same methods are used off the British Columbia coast.
Reference has been made to a council that would deal with air pollution, but I think its terms of reference are too narrow. The United States sends its people to Burlington to see what is going on, and they give us full marks for what we are doing and say we are ahead of them.
The United States has had to cut back its anti-pollution programs in big cities that pollute Lake Erie, such as Detroit, Cleveland, Buffalo and Toledo, since they are finding them too expensive. I talked about this with my friend the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher), a while ago and he admitted that we have to cut back too. Much as we would like these anti-pollution devices, we have to keep people warm and we are using more gasoline. Therefore, we must set up certain priorities. We have an excellent research council and good university programs all across Canada. We are not behind the United States or any other country in our attempts to beat this problem. The biggest culprit is the internal combustion engine. It runs on gasoline and the sooner we get an alternative, such as an engine run on hydrogen, the better. A lot of countries are working on this problem today.
As has been suggested, municipal waste is a huge problem. In Massachusetts today there is a plant that separates glass, metal, paper, food and other things found in garbage. Enough money is made from selling this waste glass and metal to run the plant at a profit and to use the residue as combustible material to fuel an electricity plant. This is a wonderful thing. Our own energy department is aware of it, but it is a long-term project. Nevertheless, it is a good way to dispose of our garbage. Enough power is derived from it to light the homes and streets of the municipality and it accounts for a large percentage of total electricity requirements. We should do further research into making use of our waste and making sure it is turned into something that will provide fuel and power at no additional expense to the taxpayer.
Another point I want to emphasize is that pollution controls on cars, smokestacks and so on can be lifted temporarily. We are not choking yet. In certain cities like Los Angeles the pollution is bad, and none of us likes pollution, but I do not think we should get excited about it when we have an energy crisis.

Mr. Speaker, just before five o'clock I believe I had reached the point of revealing the story regarding finances and expenditures of certain political parties. I had quoted from the paper by Professor Paltiel and had dealt with the part relating to the Liberal and Conservative parties as a prelude to chapter 3 which concerns the New Democratic Party. The pertinent part which I want to quote now says:
Manifestly, the two old major Canadian parties were amply supplied with monetary resources in the 1972 campaign and to a degree the New Democratic Party as well experienced a sizeable gain in revenues and spending at the federal office level in the 1972 campaign. While miniscule in comparison with its two leading competitors, this growth permitted the party to wage a campaign replete with airplane tours and media expenditures, similar in shape if not in dimensions with that of its rivals. In comparison with the 1968 campaign expenses of the NDP federal office totalling $216,100, 1972 election expenses at the national party level were $370,644-
A quick calculation with regard to the limits contemplated in the bill show, I think, that those limits are about 11 or 12 times greater than the expenditures made by the NDP. Therefore, so far as we are concerned that limit is inordinately high and unreachable. New Democratic Party expenditures are listed under candidates' deposits, organization, travel organizers, telephone, printing costs, leader's tour, survey, contingencies, and so on. There is an item here under "bad debts", which is something neither the Liberals nor the Conservatives seemed to be bothered with. Including the media expenses, contingencies and so on, the expenditure totals $370,000. I think he indicates something very significant here in terms of the strong difference of structure which exists between the NDP and other parties, because within our budget as listed here there is an item of $84,000 for provincial quotas, that is, the provincial sections of the NDP raise money toward a budget. They raise this money on a quota basis toward a budget at the federal level for federal expenditure. Professor Paltiel points out the significance of this by saying the following:
The provincial revenue quotas are symbolic of the fact that in contrast to the major parties, the NDP is financed from the bottom up with both individual and affiliated (trade union) membership
December 20, 1973

fees being paid jointly to the provincial and federal parties, with the former being charged with the support of the latter rather than the reverse.
In other words, within the NDP we are truly a community and constituency-based political organization, a people's party in the full sense of the word. We finance the operation of our party from the community to the provincial level and the federal level, which means the national party. The membership dues I pay go to help maintain the federal office. Conversely, as the financial analysis indicates, the Liberals and Tories collect their money at the top in large chunks and finance the party from the top down. So there is control at the top by large financial contributions.
In the reverse situation, the NDP operates quite differently. There is indicated here, as well, a listing of income for the year 1972 to the federal office of the party through individual and sustaining memberships. That means individual Canadian citizens can belong to the NDP by paying a membership fee voluntarily and by saying they will sustain and finance the party either through an individual or sustaining membership. The sustaining membership may vary from province to province because each province sets what it calls sustaining memberships. In British Columbia at one time it was a minimum of $1 a month. If you become a member and agree to contribute $1 a month you are classified as a sustaining member. The membership, individual and sustaining, in 1972 accounted for $102,000 in membership fees, just about half the total income of the national office. We even had some money at one stage on deposit, and there is an amount of $763 for interest.
Then there is a list of federal general fund expenditures which are related to the convention of the NDP. This list is filed with the federal convention of the NDP every two years and is in fact public information. We are, in terms of disclosure of the source of funds, the only political party that has steadfastly indicated that anybody can obtain this information at any hour-don't come around at three o'clock in the morning because you will have some difficulty getting hold of the treasurer-by looking at the financial records of the party. We regretted this on one occasion in British Columbia, in a sense, when we were taken up on that offer by some newspaper men. They spent so much time in our provincial office during the course of the campaign that they interfered with the conduct of the provincial campaign. Nevertheless, the books were open to them.
Information concerning the source of funds is available to everybody. We have continued to hold that position because we believe that if we are in the business of dealing with the public, the public should know what we are doing and such information should not be hidden behind the fence. We believe in these principles and this is the reason we are moving these amendments in respect of campaign financing. We believe this should apply to all parties. Professor Paltiel further states:
Unfortunately no information has been obtained concerning national level expenditures of the Social Credit (Creditiste) movement in the 1972 campaign.
There was no information available, and no disclosure to Professor Paltiel. This is fine; it is the business of the national Social Credit Party if it does not wish to disclose

All I was reading to the hon. gentleman was what Professor Paltiel said. I do not give any other credence to it. I only know that Professor Paltiel made a careful examination of this- subject and it seems passing strange to me that suddenly, months after this document has been known, members of the Social Credit Party in the House rise and say that that was not proven. Maybe that is why the hon. member for Abitibi does not know what is going on between his party and ITT and other groups of that sort.

I submit, judging from the financial information that has been given out, that in fact these are not limitations. You cannot call it a limitation when you place a limit 2 'A to three times the level reached by a particular party, namely, the government party in this case, or twice as much so far as the official opposition is concerned-twice as high as the level they reached just last year. That is not in fact a limitation; it is simply some kind of formula that will permit the Liberal Party to run around the country and say, "Look how grand we are. Look how good and pure we are. We brought in a bill that limits campaign expenditures." That is a lot of rot. This bill does not limit campaign expenditures in the least. The way inflation is going, it may limit campaign expenditures some day in the future; but it will not now and it will not at the next federal election when a party such as the Liberal Party spends at the federal level, as it declared it did, the sum of $1,321,000.
They spend that sum of money and then turn around and say that they want to limit campaign expenditures at the national level by imposing a limit of $4.2 million. That is no limitation; they can squander another $3 million on leader's tours, surveys and other things that go on during an election campaign, and still not reach the limit stated in the bill. The Conservative Party does likewise. So far as the financial experience and history of the NDP is concerned, we will probably never reach that level of expenditure. The total limitation is in the neighbourhood of $11 million for the national campaign. All that excessive expenditure means to the two old-line parties is that they are intent upon following the notion that the more money you spend, the greater is the possibility of buying votes. Certainly that is wrong in our democratic structure, in my view.

They deal with the highly important principle introduced into Canadian federal legislation for the first time, that there should be limits on expenditures by parties as well as limits on expenditures by individual candidates. This is something which we have tried to achieve for a long time, and we are glad to see the principle stated in the section that we are discussing to which the present amendments seek a further amendment. They seek a further amendment for the purpose of making the limitation a rational one.
I concur entirely with the remarks made by my colleague, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), that if you set the limit so high that it encourages even greater expenditures than in the past, you are not really setting a limit at all. I had thought that one of the basic purposes of this legislation, in the interest of fairness and so that money should not be a major consideration in the election of members of parliament, was to cut down the expenditures to be made in respect of elections. But the figure that we have here of 30 cents for each voter in Canada, or at least in the constituencies represented by the particular party, means-as the hon. member has pointed out- expenditures of at least $4 million in addition to some of the other expenditures which he listed and which I will not repeat.
In our view, that is no limitation at all; in fact, it is a farce to talk about limiting campaign expenditures, to say that this is one of the purposes of the legislation and then to set the limit so high that it is no real limitation at all-it is a move upward rather than a move downward. The parliamentary secretary in a discussion on a radio program with me today said, and he is quite right, that there is nothing particularly sacrosanct about the figure of 30 cents, nor is there about the other figures we have mentioned in the three amendments. One amendment brought in by the hon. member for Skeena provides for a reduction to 15 cents. The amendment I have introduced strikes a happy mean at 20 cents, and for some reason or other the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) has been rather conservative and has said that we should restrict it to 25 cents.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rather sympathetic to the viewpoint of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) who I know has had an interest in this subject for a long time. I agree that I was being overly generous. The government said 30 cents. We would like any kind of compromise on that figure. I would be prepared to support the figure suggested by the hon. member for Greenwood, and even more pleased to support the figure suggested by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). The hon. member for Skeena cuts it in half. That probably means a contribution from the federal treasury of about $1,100,000 to the federal parties, and an over-all sum of $2,100,000 is not a small contribution to make on behalf of the parties. But really when one looks at the amount of money necessary to run an election, one begins to wonder.
We have gone both ways on this particular subject. There was a time in England under the British parliamentary system when a person had to have a certain amount of money before he could become a candidate for office. Over the years it was decided that that was not the kind of limitation which should be placed on people and on the representatives of people. But it is still the type of limitation that is in force with respect to becoming a member of the Senate. It is surprising how many people in Canada today have enough money to meet the criteria to become senators. I believe one has to own $4,000 worth of property. I remember the case of one person appointed to the Senate: he did not have $4,000 and had to borrow it from a finance company on the strength of the salary he was going to get as a senator.
There is no question that over the years many people elected to this House have had to go in hock to finance companies in order to get enough money to run their campaigns. There have been occasions when a constituency organization in my party has had to go to a bank and make a personal loan to one or two people to finance an election campaign. In some cases this is necessary, and may even be desirable. During the depression years, when money was very scarce, people were desperately looking for candidates to represent them rather than the institutions which they believed were causing their difficulties. I well remember one of my constituents telling me he participated in an election in 1933 in one of the poorer sections of the dust bowl in Saskatchewan. He and some of his friends went out and cut cord wood, loaded it on a flat car and sold it for $2 a cord to get enough to finance part of the campaign for J. S. Woodsworth. He also told me about riding around the country on horseback raising money for the local candidate. We have come a long way from that situation because through this bill we are saying that $4.2 million should be provided by the treasury for the conduct of an election.
Of course, this is not a large sum of money when compared with what was spent by the parties in the last
Election Expenses
general election. Paltiel indicates that the last election cost at least a reported $32 million and may have cost considerably more when the government's expenses in connection with the election machinery are included. I think I have seen the figure of $11 million mentioned to cover that operation. Thus it can be seen that elections are a very expensive proposition. For this reason alone it may be necessary for the treasury to provide money to run elections. If this is so, then I suggest that we start off with as low an amount as possible, and that we put strong limitations on various aspects so that elections do not run into multimillion dollar figures but, rather, that election expenses are reduced to the point where they can be easily scrutinized either by the agent who is going to be appointed or by the auditors who will be going over the accounts of the various candidates.
It is my personal opinion that we would be well advised to provide the individual candidate with the opportunity to mail something to the electors in his riding at a cost of about 8 cents to 10 cents per name, but given in kind rather than through this type of arrangement which could lend itself more to the expansion of expenditures by national political parties than to a reduction of expenditures.
We have heard a lot of argument on how political parties are financed. How the New Democratic Party has been financed has never been a secret. It has been financed by people who had a problem and who decided to join together to end that problem. It is interesting to read in Paltiel's report of the last election of something that surprised him, namely, that the amount of money the NDP gets between elections varies very little from year to year, indicating that the party's supporters are willing to make the same kind of contribution each year in order to see that the party continues as their political spokesman.
The other political parties have tended to adopt more elite ways of raising money. It is interesting to look at the direction in which they are going. A history of the last several elections in the United States shows that the Republicans, the Democrats, and even the Wallace campaign adopted several methods of raising money. In the final analysis, most of these methods of raising money created almost as many problems as they were able to solve with the money that they received. They have included fund raising dinners; this has been copied in Canada, sometimes successfully and sometimes not so successfully. In most cases where they are successful an organization is hired to make the arrangements for setting up the dinner and they are paid a certain proportion of the proceeds for running it. In the United States I gather they were paid 7 per cent or 8 per cent of the net take. These have been fairly successful in the United States but I do not know whether political parties in Canada have gone into fund raising to this extent.
There is a second method that can be bought and of course it has a price, and that is direct mailing. They do not direct mail to all the constituents but have a very elaborate system through which they buy names that they believe would be advantageous. In the last United States election the Democratic Party bought lists of names that were involved in causes-anti-war, anti-poverty and two

December 20, 1973
Election Expenses
or three of the major protest groups. These turned out to be as good fund raising propositions from a business point of view as did the normal register of Democratic voters. On the other hand, the Republican Party found that selecting names by the computer operation at so much a name was much more satisfactory.
This all leads to the problem that most political parties are faced with today, Mr. Speaker, and that is running an election by computer in a computerized society. In the last presidential election in the United States they were able to raise so much money that they had $3 million or $4 million left over. This was available for other purposes, so some bright young people were given sums of money and told to do something with it that would have an effect on the election. They did something with it that had an effect on the election that was overwhelmingly successful but also overwhelmingly disastrous. It was disastrous for the people who did it because of the corruption involved, and it was disastrous for all political parties in the United States and in Canada because of the results that flowed from the use of that extra money.
An election cannot be conducted without money, and it certainly behooves us to have enough money available to at least have the message of a candidate, no matter whether he has a chance of winning, put before the public. To that degree the payment of a sum of money from the treasury is a good thing. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I think there should be a limitation on that expenditure except for the contribution that an individual wishes to make in a particular riding. As they say, it is true that you have to show the flag in areas where a political party may not have much strength. The Conservatives are having this problem in the province of Quebec-they have joined the New Democratic Party which has had the same problem in that province for many years. My guess is that the Conservatives will be no more successful in showing the flag in Quebec than we have been, but I think it is a fact that they have to do it. If I were a Liberal, I would be scared that neither the New Democratic Party nor the Conservatives are successful in the province of Quebec because that might be to their detriment rather than to their advantage.

speechtext:
We have been able to show the flag for many years in that province, but his party has not done very well there although they may have done a little better than they did in Quebec. However, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to go through all the provinces. We have had very little success in a number of them ourselves, and I do not see any sense in throwing rocks. I suggest that it is a fact of politics that you have to present, as a party, the image of being available in those areas. It is a fact that if people in other parts of Canada believe that a political party is worth while, then you should at least have the right to put forth your program to people in other parts of the country. For this reason I am sympathetic to the idea of providing a sum of money.
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that this should have been mixed up with so many other considerations for I would like this bill to have contained a clause somewhat along the lines that have been suggested; a total, inescapable report clause that would have made it mandatory to make honest reports. It is interesting to note that we have always allowed those people who have lost to get by without making any kind of report. I believe that if the name of the game is to provide reasonable contributions so that the stories of candidates who have something to say can be told across the country, and if a contribution from the treasury will make that possible we should support it. It should be reasonable; it should not be an excessive amount of money. I believe that not too many years ago $4.2 million would have been more than most political parties considered elections should cost. Costs have escalated to the point where we are now spending well over $30 million each election and they are costing $10 million or $11 million to operate. It indicates that we have not kept pace with modern thinking when we allow expenses to go so high.
Mr. Speaker, if that $4.2 million is properly distributed I think there will be an opportunity for some organizations which feel they would like to become political parties to do so. I have been impressed with the way political parties are formed almost overnight. Sometimes they disappear just as quickly, of course. I am thinking, for instance, of the teachers of this nation who a few years ago were all status quo people and never objected whatever the government did. In British Columbia they embraced the Social Credit Party with open arms and loved them to death until that government suddenly decided there was going to be compulsory arbitration. I have been in many schools in Ontario where press releases from Queen's Park were prominently displayed on the bulletin board and were required reading for all the teachers. There certainly was no resentment about that.
We might well see a new political movement started by some of the so-called white collar workers and professional people of the nation. I sincerely hope we are not making it difficult for them to enter the political arena, run as candidates and get their message across to the public. It seems to me that 30 cents is too high. I should like the government to consider 15 cents, which I believe is a reasonable amount. I would be prepared to support the proposition of the hon. member for Greenwood that it be 20 cents.
December 20, 1973

What we should avoid is getting ourselves into the position the Americans have done. Give us the money, they say, and we can win an election. I was pleased to note that despite these circumstances south of the border, a third party was able to make an impact during the last presidential election there without the funds available to the two major parties. I was pleased that a third party was able to champion a number of causes and rally round it people who were often of dissimilar views but who were ready to support a group which would allow individuals to make a contribution to the political scene without the backing of large sums of money.
Mr. Paltiel indicates that the Conservative Party assessed the possibilities of 50 ridings in Ontario and chose a number to be visited by the leader himself as part of a special attempt to increase support in those ridings. We, too, have hired people to assess the possibilities of ridings and determine in which of them candidates might best be run, and I am sure all political parties have done the same. No people are worse copycats then politicians: if one thinks of something good, another will immediately seek to copy it. We need look no further than the publications which individual members send to their constituents. If someone gets hold of a copy which appears to contain a new idea or involves a new format, it is immediately picked up.
I believe the country would be prepared to see a contribution made to candidates, even a $4 million contribution, if they were sure this was all the election would cost. It may be I get my contributions from the men who work in the mines, or in industry, or on the farms. The other two political parties may get their money from the men who run the multinational corporations. But in the end the money will all come from the men at the bottom. It is they who will pay it, either directly or indirectly. In one case, though, a person makes a donation knowing what he is doing and believing that to do so is in his interest. In the other case they are making an indirect contribution and one which very often will be used against them rather than for them. For these reasons I hope the House will accept the amendment calling for 15 cents.

speechtext: My hon. friend brings it down to 10 cents. That sounds like a nice round figure. I wish he had been here when the amendments were being made; he could have moved a reduction to 10 cents. I am aware that it does not go directly to the candidates, but a politician would be very naive if he did not believe that a contribution made to the central party did not give him at least some measure of political advantage, whether in recognition by the news media or in other ways. I therefore hope the minister responsible for the bill will consider reducing this figure of 30 cents which I and my colleagues believe to be unnecessarily large and not really required for the effective conduct of an election.

Not really, Mr. Speaker. I was rising to speak to the motion, but I will deal with the point of order. This arose in the committee as a result of the examination of the definition of "election expenses". It relates to the question of amounts paid as election expenses. The definition of "election expenses" is given on page 2 of the bill and is:
(a)	amounts paid,
(b)	liabilities incurred
(e) the commercial value of goods-
And so on. The words we are concerned with here are "amounts paid". Since I knew the practice existed in varying degrees in different parties, I asked whether the words "amounts paid" included donations or contributions or gifts or transfers of money paid out of the national treasury to constituency associations, the official agent in constituency associations, candidates and so on. Initially I thought it would be included because it was an amount paid out of the treasury of the federal branch of the party concerned. As the definition says further on, one of the purposes of these amounts was to promote or oppose directly, and during an election, a particular registered party, or the election of a particular candidate.
The minister in charge of the bill, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), said no, that was not the intention of the definition of election expenses; the intention was that contributions, donations or gifts from the central funds of the party paid to a candidate or official agent were not to be included in the election expenses. Just in case there was any doubt about it, he said that the government proposed to put into the bill later on an amendment to make doubly sure that this was not to be included. The amendment put in is the one we are now seeking to amend.

speechtext:
I would have thought that my hon. friend from Mississauga (Mr. Blenkarn) would have been delighted with my grammatical construction in that sentence, which would reflect the education I have received as a result of sitting next to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who advises us on these matters. The amendment I am seeking to amend is shown on page 9 of the bill. This is the amendment that the government put forward in the committee to clarify and to make sure beyond the shadow of a doubt that this kind of expenditure was not included in the "amounts paid" part of the definition of election expenses. Section (1.1) reads as follows:

In determining, for the purposes of this section, the amount of election expenses incurred by a registered party on account of or in respect of the conduct or management of an election, there shall not be included any amount in respect of contributions or gifts made by or on behalf of the registered party for the use of candidates at the election.
One way to approach this problem would be to vote against section (1.1.), which would remove it from the bill. I say this because, at the very best, there would be doubt as to whether these would be contributions or gifts made by or on behalf of the registered party for the use of the candidate. We would leave in doubt whether contributions should or should not be included under amounts paid for election expenses.
Certainly there was doubt about this in the minister's mind or he would not have brought forward the change in the first place. Certainly there was doubt in my mind, which is understandable; but then there is also doubt in my mind about all kinds of other questions. There is doubt in my mind as to what "amounts paid" might mean. I know that there was doubt in the mind of the cabinet minister responsible for drafting this bill. He said in so many words, "Yes, there is doubt in my mind." He suggested that the relevant portion should be changed. The parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Kenora-Rai-ny River (Mr. Reid), moved the motion and it carried. He was a member of the committee. He wanted to insert the particular clause in question.
I submit that if we negative it, remove it completely, there will be continuing uncertainty as to whether or not such contributions as I have alluded to should be included under amounts paid. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), the sponsor of this motion, looked at this question carefully. We discussed it among ourselves. We wondered what was the best approach and in the end we felt that an amendment simply to take out the word "not" would be the best way of handling it. The result would not be a direct negative, inasmuch as we should be left with a positive declaration that for the purposes of this section we could determine what are election expenses incurred by a registered party. We would remove any doubt about it. People would know what is meant by amounts paid as defined in the definition section. They would know what those words mean in relation to expenditures. They would know that certain items should be included under amounts paid and certain expenses should be so included. That would be a positive declaration. They would know that there shall be included under amounts paid any amount in respect of a contribution or gift made by or on behalf of the party.
It could not be done the other way, I submit, as much uncertainty would be the result. After all, not all candidates, official agents or chief agents who will perform their functions under this law-incidentally, I hope this will not be the law-will have sat on the committee and heard the involved and detailed discussions that took place. Members in the committee and in the House have alluded to the fantastic input which the committee had in connection with this bill. Even in the minds of committee members who spent hour after hour looking at this question there was doubt.
December 20, 1973

I submit that if we were to remove this clause we would bring about a great deal of confusion and it would be difficult to figure out what amounts should be included in returns on election expenses. We would not know what amounts of money should be included and what should not be included under amounts paid. Further, even if the parties wanted to do the right thing they would find it extremely difficult to do so. They might do the wrong thing even though they want to do the right thing. For that reason, for the sake of clarity if for no other reason, I suggest this motion must be considered as being in order.

speechtext:
The amendment before us seeks to deal with the very serious question of campaign fund expenditures. We all know that money is a pretty potent force at election time. We know there is a tendency for candidates, particularly for registered parties, to think that the more lavish they make the brochure, the more money they spend with an advertising agency in preparing television plugs and spots, the more the political parties concerned can sell its image. They tend to draw a distinction in the sense of image which is not very credible. There is an attempt to develop mechanisms that are not designed to promote public discussion, to establish conversation in the community or to enlighten people about the issues in the campaign.
We all know this. No party is very different from another in that regard. They are designed to influence, to manipulate or to have an effect. They are designed to be attractive primarily to the apolitical voter; they are designed primarily for that person in our society, and there are quite a number of them. By my assessment, 20 per cent to 25 per cent of those who vote are within the group that has the general reference apolitical. These people do not pay attention to politics. The campaign expenditures are designed to have an impact upon or influence that type of voter. That type of voter has no sort of involvement or connection with the political process because he does not generally pay any attention whatsoever to politics, government, legislative items, policies, or who did or did not do what in the political arena. It is considered that he is likely to be influenced at the emotional level more than at the mental level, the level of thought, analysis and logic.
We know that it costs a good deal more in production and agency fees if someone is hired to work out a slick, smooth 30-second television shot designed with no other thought in mind than to impress or make an impact upon the voter. One would pay a good deal more for this type of television program than for the more honest one involving a five-minute period or longer in which one converses in detail or in depth about a party's ideas, programs and policies in an attempt by this mechanism to get across a point of view or an understanding to the general public. There is a tendency not to do that sort of thing and there is a tendency toward the other, that is, toward buying advertising expertise. There is a tendency to go to those agencies which spend the whole year around developing

ads designed to sell toothpaste or underarm deodorant, or whatever else might be sold by someone who wishes to sell it.
In respect of a political party, this is regrettable. This is not necessarily a severe criticism of a political party but it is a sad commentary, I think, upon the level of political demand in the country if a political party feels it should go to an agency and ask it to make up a package for it, but rather than call it Crest, call it NDP; do not call it Arrid but call it Liberal or whatever. Just substitute the political party's name for the name of the mouthwash and sell it in the same way. That costs a lot of money.

Mr. Speaker, sometimes I cannot hear these comments and I let them go by. But seriously, in reponse to the previous question, what is involved is simply that there is a provision in the bill, that we just dealt with, that says the limitation on campaign expenditures by political parties shall not exceed 30 cents times the number of voters in those ridings within which they run candidates. The key words are that that "election expenses" shall not exceed that amount of money, whatever the multiplication comes to.
We have the figure of roughly $4.2 million if parties run candidates in all ridings. When the matter was being considered by the committee we inquired, with respect to the definition of election expenses, whether or not within that definition there was to be included the amount of money that a registered party, or the central headquarters of a party, the national office or whatever they want to call it, gave as donations or contributions to the various constituencies and candidates. This has ranged anywhere from $4,000 to $7,000 in some areas, averaging $5,000 to $6,000 per candidate for the two old-line parties. There was doubt in the committee whether or not that type of expenditure by a national party was to be included within the definition of election expenses. The President of the Privy Council said so, that it was not to include that. If other words, the limitation on election expenses would be 30 cents times the number of voters on the list, plus whatever a political party wanted to donate to its respective candidates running under its banner in the particular ridings. And for more clarity he moved this amendment, which is now before us as 13.(2) (1.1) on page 9 of the bill, and which says:
In determining, for the purposes of this section, the amount of election expenses incurred by a registered party on account of or in respect of the conduct or the management of an election, there shall not be included any amount in respect of contributions or gifts made by or on behalf of the registered party for the use of candidates at the election.
We seek to take the "not" out of that so that when it is removed it will clearly say that the 30 cents times the number of voters on the voters' list, whatever total that comes to, will include the contributions that the party makes to its registered candidates. In other words it would have the effect, within the 30 cents factor, of limiting that by the amount the party contributes to candidates. I do not know whether Hansard got the last interjection, Mr. Speaker, but the hon. member for Greenwood said that I have got him convinced. So I have got his vote tied up tight. Now I have only to convince some 260 other members of the House.
Looking, for argument's sake, at the Liberal Party, Mr. Speaker, this would not affect the campaign fund expenditures of that party one iota because in the last federal election they expended $1,321,989 to cover radio time and television time, printed media and other advertising, leader's tour, travel, surveys, administration and the like, and in addition to that contributed something in the neighbourhood of $5,000 on the average per candidate running for the Liberal Party.
On just a very rough estimate of $5,000 times 264 candidates, that came to something in the neighbourhood of $1.3 million. So that in addition to the other $1.3 million they spent in the last election campaign, they could make this

$5,000 contribution or donation to each one of the candidates running for the Liberal Party and only come to an amount of $2.6 million, which would still leave ample room for expansion within the $4.2 million available according to the formula in the bill.
I know that revealing this kind of information about a $5,000 contribution on average from the national headquarters of the Liberal Party has caused a number of Liberal members in the House to raise their eyebrows and look in my direction. Obviously they are the ones who did not get $5,000; they got much less. Maybe at that time they were not in favour with the leader of the party, and he figured that if he cut back on these contributions they would not have much chance of getting at him. It is obvious that he did that with a number of members of the previous parliament because they were defeated in that campaign.

With respect to the PC party, again talking in terms of what is indicated with regard to their activities, they also would not be affected one bit because their total expenditure, according to Mr. Finlay MacDonald who was, and maybe still is, their national campaign chairman at the time he provided this information, total PC national office expenditures in the 1972 campaign were $4,520,321 which, if the 30 cents formula were applied, would be just about right where the limit was; and that included the amounts of money allocated to constituencies, or remitted to constituencies, and Professor Paltiel points out that the constituency allocations appeared to average out at $6,600.
Some provinces and their constituencies, like Alberta, were entirely self-sustaining. So what the total contribution was is hard to say from that, except that Mr. MacDonald does say that the total remittance to provincial allotments and constituencies was some $1,748,000-that was the national campaign-bringing it up to a total of $4.1 million.
If we are seriously concerned about trying to effectively and reasonably limit campaign expenses, then we should be thinking seriously about either limiting or reducing the amount of that 30 cents. That can be done by one of those deferred divisions or by taking out the word "not" and saying that we had reached the peak. Both the Liberals and Conservatives, by their own statements, had concluded that that was a peak expenditure last time, and it was a peak position in so far as finding the flow of campaign contributions to the treasury is concerned. I think they will find that the more campaigns cost, the more difficult it will be to raise money. I know that is true of my own constituency and the organization to which I belong. We have found it more and more difficult all the time to raise money.

Certainly next week. In fact, I may have the answers next week. I do not have all the answers right now. Mr. Speaker, that is why we have difficulty in raising money. A few years ago in my constituency I looked at the returns the other candidates had filed. I am sure they looked at mine, and that is all right. I looked at the return filed by the Liberal Party and the return for that campaign within the constituency run by the Liberal Party, and the Liberal candidate showed an expenditure of $5,000-odd. It showed one contribution exactly equal to the expenditures, and the source of that contribution was the Liberal Federation of Canada. I know that the Liberal Party raised money in Skeena in the election campaign, but I do not know where it went. I also know that a lot of Liberal Party members in that riding would like to know because the Liberal Federation of Canada paid the whole shot.
The Conservative Party received contributions some years ago, too. The Conservative candidate in the riding listed his source of campaign funds and one was a contribution of $2,000 or $4,000 from one Frederick Field, and accountant in Vancouver. When the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was Prime Minister and had some authority for appointments, lo and behold, shortly after the election this Frederick Field was made a member of the board of the Bank of Canada and the Industrial Development Bank. We raised the question and Mr. Field said, and I gather quite rightly, "Good heavens; I thought I got here on merit and not by any contribution". It turned out that Frederick Field was simply the treasurer of the Conservative Party in British Columbia at that time. The Conservative candidate had make an error and

instead of listing the Conservative Association, or whatever it was, he listed Frederick Field because that was who signed the cheque. It really did not come from Frederick Field at all, but from some unknown source.
We have to seriously face the question of whether we are really concerned about continuing to think that the more money we spend, to more we will be able to influence voters. To continue in that direction, I submit, tends to demean us as individuals, tends to demean political parties and tends to place them in the same class as mouthwash and toothpaste companies. Instead of being the Progressive Conservative Party, it might be Proctor-Gamble next time, or whoever makes those sorts of things. That will be the name that will appear by mistake. The advertising agency, instead of saying "Vote Progressive Conservative" will be saying "Vote Proctor-Gamble". It will not make much difference to the advertising agency which advertises the idea.

Mr. Speaker, on December 6 I asked the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) if he knew where Mississauga was and how it could conceivably take five days for a letter send special delivery and express, with a 40-cent stamp on it, to come from Regina, Saskatchewan, to Mississauga. There is at least one direct flight per day by Air Canada from Regina to Mississauga. On November 21 a Mrs. Stutt went into the Regina head office of the post office of this government in Regina, Saskatchewan, and deposited with the postmaster's clerk there a letter marked "Special Delivery" and "Express" containing four Grey Cup tickets. Five days later, one day after the Grey Cup had been played at Toronto, that special delivery, express letter was delivered by the postmaster's servant to my constituents, Mr. and Mrs. Douglas Robb in Mississauga.
In answering that question, the postmaster said he was going to spend a lot of money on the Gateway post office in Mississauga: that was the only answer he had. Sir, citizens of this country, relying on the monopoly system of postal delivery, supposedly guaranteed, having spent 40 cents, not 8 cents, on a special delivery express letter,

having spoken to the clerk in the main office in the post office in Regina, find that their letters took five complete days to be delivered-more than five if one counts the whole of the period between the 21st and the 26th. I repeat, this was a letter marked "Special Delivery, "Express" on which a 40-cent stamp had been placed, and there is a direct airline service between the two centres at least once a day.
That is about the worst case I have come across, but it is not the only case. At least once or twice a week I personally write to the Postmaster General, and my constituency office writes to the postmaster's officials in Mississauga several times a week with respect to the kind of mail service the city of Mississauga receives. I want to remind the Postmaster General that Mississauga is larger than the city of Victoria, the capital of British Columbia; that it is larger than St. John's, the capital of Newfoundland; that it is larger than Regina, the capital city of Saskatchewan; larger by far than the city of Charlottetown, the capital of Prince Edward Island; and larger, indeed, than the City of Quebec which is the capital of the fair province of Quebec. Nevertheless, this city receives a postal service upon which the major industries within it cannot rely.
I have communicated to the Postmaster General evidence from the St. Lawrence Cement Company that it takes six days for special delivery of documentation to Mississauga from Chicago. Indeed, the St. Lawrence Cement Company has advised me that in no circumstances would it trust the Post Office of Canada; it would prefer to use the services of special bank courriers for the delivery of mail and important documentation.
Sometimes we in Canada cannot get too enthusiastic about the difficulties facing commercial organizations. After all, they only meet huge payrolls and pay enormous taxes to support such ineffective operations as I have been describing! There are people like Helen Friese who delivered evidence to me showing that it took mail from July 14 to September 10 to get from Port Credit to Toronto.

I have also received information from councillors of the city of Mississauga that even within the city mail sometimes takes six days to go from the sub-post office at Port Credit to the sub-post office at Malton. There are people who have been residents in my community since it was called the township of Toronto. They bring me evidence that mail in that part of the city of Mississauga still served by rural delivery usually takes seven days to come from Toronto.
This sort of thing goes on and on. Every time I write the Postmaster General about the kind of service Canadians expect, that people in a developed urban location like the city of Mississauga are entitled to receive from their government, I get wishy-washy, beautiful letters. Sometimes the department sends its officials to talk to my constituents. They give them the finest of soft soap. If they would spend half the effort on service that they spend on soft soaping and advertising their new direct service, their guaranteed delivery system, their wonderful six-letter codes, and give this community the kind of service it received with the pony express prior to the steam engine, we would be happy.

Mr. Speaker, I would briefly remind the hon. member that Toronto Post Office employees are handling about 5 million pieces of mail a day. I would also remind the hon. member that at this time of the year the employees of my department are handling about 10 million pieces of mail a day. Of course, we admit that errors are possible and I would like the hon. member to think that with a percentage of errors of only one per cent about 200,000 people would be entitled to complain for late mail.
I think that the hon. member has been slightly exaggerating in his speech and if he is in a position to give a few examples of errors I am convinced that with some goodwill he will find that the mailing services have been quite efficient in hundreds of cases. Perhaps he forgets that for one delayed letter 99 others are delivered on time. I think I should also emphasize that throughout the Post Office administration the improvement of our service depends to a large extent on factors independent from my department such as weather, road conditions and delayed planes or trains which are so many factors liable to influence the punctuality of mail deliveries.
There is also the fact that human nature is fallible and mistakes are bound to happen in the handling of mail. But I do not think that the hon. member is in a position to complain mainly because he is from Mississauga and that in reply to his letter I informed him on December 6 that precisely in Mississauga, we would build an ultra-modern post office to sort out the mail automatically, help improve considerably the mail handling and make that service much more efficient.
To my mind, the hon. member must think that everything works properly, under normal conditions. I urge him to make a personal inquiry. He gives me as an example a letter mailed from Regina which reached its destination too late. If tthe hon. member mails his letter before 11 a.m. in Regina, one can normally guarantee delivery in Mississauga on the next day; if the letter is mailed after 11 a.m., in the same city, it will not normally reach its destination the day after the next. In closing, I therefore say to the hon. member that, in most cases, we respect the time limits we set ourselves. When delays occur, unfortunately, we apologize for them. We strive earnestly to improve the service.
